metadata.title: The Role of Subnational Governments in Adult Skills Systems: Iceland

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note does not analyze student microdata from an ILSA (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS) and therefore does not define a sampling frame, student-level analytic dataset, or any complex survey weighting scheme. The document describes governance structures and allocation of responsibilities across national and subnational actors in Iceland’s adult skills system (VET, HVET, CET/CVT, AE, and ALMPs). As a result, there are no plausible values (PV) or scaling procedures, and no replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) to apply. For any future quantitative evaluation using ILSA microdata, analysts would need to use the official student/sampling weights provided by the relevant dataset and apply replicate weights if variance estimation is required; this note itself provides no such variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this document is a governance and policy description of Iceland’s adult skills system rather than an empirical analysis of ILSA cognitive achievement outcomes. There is also no missing-data strategy to report because no student-level dataset, item responses, or model-based estimation is conducted in the note. The tables summarize institutional responsibilities and expenditure structure, not statistical estimation requiring PVs or missing-data handling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used a qualitative/policy description approach for Iceland’s adult skills governance; no ILSA student sample is constructed or filtered.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD country note provides a descriptive overview of how Iceland’s adult skills system is governed across national and subnational levels. It reports the governance structure (centralised system with local municipalities as subnational actors) and the allocation of responsibilities across policy areas: VET, HVET, CET/CVT, AE, and ALMPs. The note specifies which institutions lead strategy, intelligence, implementation, funding, and delivery at each governance level, including ministries, national agencies, social partners, and municipal bodies. It also describes how responsibilities are operationalised through contracted coordination (e.g., the Education and Training Service Centre) and deconcentrated local offices for employment services. No ILSA/NAEP/PIRLS/PISA microdata are analysed, so there are no achievement benchmarks, model performance metrics, or statistical uncertainty estimates reported.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical large-scale assessment study: it is a policy/governance country note summarising institutional roles and expenditure structure. Consequently, there is no student-level dataset, no sampling design, no PV-based achievement outcome, and no ML model training or predictive evaluation to extract. The absence of main findings and confounders is therefore by design rather than a reporting gap.
